title: Week 8 · Lesson 22: Oncology Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 8 — Lesson 22: Oncology Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning

FNP-level goal: Use tumor biology to recognize concerning presentations, distinguish screening from diagnostic evaluation, interpret common cancer-related patterns, coordinate timely workup and referral, and identify oncologic emergencies that are unsafe for routine outpatient follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how oncogenes, tumor-suppressor loss, and DNA-repair failure contribute to carcinogenesis.
  • Differentiate benign growth, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, invasive cancer, and metastasis.
  • Recognize warning patterns that require diagnostic evaluation rather than reassurance or delayed screening.
  • Use a mechanism-based approach to cancer-related anemia, weight loss, pain, thrombosis, and paraneoplastic findings.
  • Identify red flags for spinal cord compression, febrile neutropenia, tumor lysis syndrome, malignant hypercalcemia, superior vena cava syndrome, and malignant obstruction.

Part 1 — Cancer Is a Disease of Dysregulated Cell Behavior

Cancer is not one disease. It is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells acquire the ability to grow when they should not, evade normal growth limits, survive despite damage, invade tissue, and sometimes spread to distant organs.

Normal tissue homeostasis requires a balance between cell division, differentiation, DNA repair, senescence, and programmed cell death. Malignancy develops when accumulated genetic and epigenetic changes disrupt that balance.

Normal growth control fails → clonal expansion → additional alterations → invasion and possible metastasis.

Part 2 — The Three Gene Categories

Three broad gene categories are especially useful for FNP-level reasoning:

  • Proto-oncogenes: normally promote controlled growth and survival. Activating changes can create oncogenes that signal growth excessively.
  • Tumor suppressor genes: normally slow the cell cycle, promote repair, or trigger cell death when damage is severe. Loss of function removes a “brake.”
  • DNA-repair genes: correct DNA damage. Defects allow mutations to accumulate and increase genomic instability.

Think: accelerator stuck on + brakes fail + repair system fails = rising malignant potential.

Part 3 — Carcinogenesis Is Usually Multistep

Most cancers emerge through multiple acquired changes over time. Mutations may result from cell-division errors, inherited susceptibility, tobacco, ultraviolet radiation, ionizing radiation, chronic inflammation, infections associated with specific cancers, or other environmental exposures. Risk is not destiny: an exposure or family history changes probability, not the diagnosis by itself.

FNP reasoning includes prevention and early recognition: assess tobacco exposure, alcohol and metabolic risk where relevant, ultraviolet exposure, vaccination history, occupational/environmental exposure, and a three-generation family history when hereditary cancer is plausible.

Part 4 — Benign, Premalignant, and Malignant Disease

Benign tumors do not invade nearby tissue or metastasize, although location can still make them clinically important. Dysplasia describes abnormal cellular maturation or architecture and can be a precursor in selected tissues. Carcinoma in situ is a neoplastic epithelial process confined above the basement membrane. Invasive cancer crosses normal tissue boundaries and may gain access to lymphatic or blood vessels.

Do not use “benign” to mean “never needs follow-up,” and do not use “abnormal” to mean “cancer.” Pathology, imaging, clinical context, and follow-up determine risk.

Part 5 — Invasion and Metastasis

For a tumor to metastasize, cells must detach, invade extracellular matrix, enter lymphatic or blood vessels, survive transit, leave the circulation, and establish a new blood supply in a distant organ. This explains why lymph nodes, liver, lungs, bone, brain, and other organs may become sites of metastatic disease depending on tumor type and route of spread.

Local mass effect causes obstruction, bleeding, pain, or compression. Metastatic disease can add systemic symptoms and organ-specific findings: focal neurologic deficits, pathologic fracture, cholestatic pattern, dyspnea, ascites, or marrow suppression.

Part 6 — Angiogenesis, Hypoxia, and Tumor Heterogeneity

A growing tumor needs oxygen and nutrients. Tumor-driven angiogenesis can support expansion, but tumor vessels are often structurally abnormal. Uneven perfusion and hypoxia can promote aggressive behavior and treatment resistance. Within one tumor, different cell populations may carry different alterations; this heterogeneity helps explain variable response and acquired resistance.

This is why a pathology report, stage, molecular findings, performance status, and treatment history matter. “Cancer” alone is not enough information to determine a safe plan.

Part 7 — Screening Is Not Diagnostic Evaluation

Screening applies to asymptomatic people at an appropriate risk level; it attempts to find disease before symptoms develop. Diagnostic evaluation applies when symptoms, examination, laboratory findings, or imaging suggest disease. A patient with rectal bleeding, a new breast mass, persistent hematuria, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia, progressive dysphagia, or postmenopausal bleeding does not simply need “routine screening.” They need timely diagnostic evaluation.

Screening recommendations change and differ by age, sex, risk, family history, prior results, and life expectancy. The FNP should use current guideline-based shared decision-making rather than memorizing one universal interval.

Part 8 — Cancer Warning Patterns in Primary Care

Concerning patterns are not diagnoses, but they should change the threshold for evaluation:

  • unintentional weight loss, persistent fatigue, anorexia, or night sweats;
  • new mass, progressive lymphadenopathy, or persistent focal bone pain;
  • new or changing skin lesion, nonhealing ulcer, or unexplained bleeding;
  • persistent cough, hemoptysis, hoarseness, dysphagia, early satiety, or change in bowel habits;
  • hematuria, postmenopausal bleeding, testicular mass, or persistent unexplained cytopenia;
  • recurrent unprovoked thrombosis or a symptom complex that does not fit a benign diagnosis.

Do not anchor on cancer alone. Infection, autoimmune disease, endocrine disease, medication effects, benign lesions, and common cardiopulmonary or GI conditions remain in the differential.

Part 9 — A Focused FNP Workup

Start with the clinical problem, not a broad “cancer panel.” Clarify time course, constitutional symptoms, bleeding, pain, bowel/bladder change, medication history, tobacco/alcohol exposure, prior cancer, radiation, immunosuppression, and family history. Complete a focused examination including lymph nodes, skin, abdomen, breast/testicular/pelvic evaluation when indicated, neurologic function, and evidence of thrombosis or obstruction.

Initial laboratory and imaging choices should answer a question: CBC and indices for anemia/cytopenias, metabolic and hepatic testing for organ impact, urinalysis for hematuria, targeted imaging for a focal symptom, and urgent referral or emergency evaluation when instability is possible. Tumor markers are not general screening tests; their value depends on a specific clinical context and should be interpreted with specialists when appropriate.

Part 10 — Cancer-Related Anemia, Weight Loss, and Pain

Anemia in a patient with cancer or an unexplained concerning syndrome may arise from occult blood loss, inflammation-related impaired iron availability, marrow infiltration, nutritional deficiency, kidney disease, hemolysis, or treatment effects. The pattern and reticulocyte response help build the differential. Do not assume fatigue is “just stress” when anemia, weight loss, bleeding, or progressive symptoms coexist.

Cancer-related weight loss may reflect reduced intake, early satiety, pain, depression, malabsorption, cytokine-driven catabolism, or treatment toxicity. Persistent focal bone pain, night pain, pain at rest, neurologic symptoms, or pathologic-fracture risk deserves prompt evaluation rather than prolonged empiric analgesic treatment alone.

Part 11 — Thrombosis and Paraneoplastic Effects

Malignancy can promote a prothrombotic state through inflammatory signaling, tumor-derived procoagulant activity, immobility, venous compression, central lines, and treatment. New unilateral leg swelling, unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, or hypoxemia requires a VTE differential; never assume symptoms are only from the known cancer.

Some tumors produce hormones, cytokines, or antibodies that cause paraneoplastic syndromes. Examples include hypercalcemia, SIADH-like hyponatremia patterns, endocrinologic changes, neurologic syndromes, or thrombotic phenomena. The FNP task is to recognize a coherent physiologic pattern and expedite evaluation, not to assign a tumor type from one laboratory result.

Part 12 — Treatment-Related Safety

Antineoplastic therapy can cause predictable but high-risk complications: myelosuppression, neutropenia, mucositis, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, cardiotoxicity, neuropathy, renal injury, hepatic injury, endocrine changes, thrombosis, and immune-related adverse events with some therapies. Medication reconciliation must include oral anticancer therapy, biologics, infusion schedules, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, antiemetics, and supplements.

A patient actively receiving treatment with fever, new dyspnea, chest pain, severe diarrhea, confusion, bleeding, severe mucositis, or inability to hydrate may need same-day oncology contact or emergency evaluation. Follow the patient’s oncology plan and local pathways; do not delay escalation while trying to determine every agent’s adverse-effect profile.

Part 13 — Oncologic Emergencies

Febrile neutropenia

Fever or systemic symptoms in a patient with significant treatment-related neutropenia can represent a rapidly progressive infection with muted local findings. It requires urgent protocol-based evaluation; it is not a routine next-day visit.

Spinal cord compression

Back pain with new weakness, sensory change, gait difficulty, saddle symptoms, or bowel/bladder dysfunction in a patient with known or suspected cancer raises concern for spinal cord compression. Time matters: arrange emergency assessment and imaging.

Malignant hypercalcemia

Hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, constipation, nausea, weakness, confusion, arrhythmia risk, and kidney injury. Severe symptoms or marked laboratory abnormality require urgent evaluation.

Tumor lysis syndrome

Rapid cell breakdown, often around initiation of treatment for susceptible malignancies, can cause dangerous potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric-acid, and kidney abnormalities. Weakness, palpitations, oliguria, or acute illness after therapy require urgent assessment.

Superior vena cava syndrome and obstruction

Facial/neck swelling, dyspnea, venous distention, headache, or upper-extremity swelling may indicate central venous obstruction. Airway symptoms, neurologic symptoms, or rapid progression require emergency care.

Part 14 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 1

A 64-year-old with a 40-pack-year history has progressive cough, 12-lb unintentional weight loss, intermittent hemoptysis, and new supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The task is not to name the final cancer in clinic. Build the problem representation: high-risk exposure + progressive pulmonary symptoms + constitutional symptoms + abnormal node.

FNP decision: arrange prompt diagnostic evaluation using local pathways and communicate red flags. If respiratory compromise, significant bleeding, or instability develops, escalate to emergency care.

Part 15 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 2

A 58-year-old with treated breast cancer reports new progressive thoracic back pain, nighttime pain, leg weakness, and urinary retention. Do not treat this as uncomplicated muscle strain.

Mechanism: metastatic vertebral disease can compress neural structures.

FNP decision: possible spinal cord compression is an emergency; arrange immediate emergency evaluation.

Part 16 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 3

A patient receiving chemotherapy calls with fever, chills, weakness, and dizziness. The absence of purulent cough or dysuria does not make the presentation safe. Treatment-related immune suppression may blunt local findings.

FNP decision: follow the oncology emergency pathway and arrange immediate evaluation for possible febrile neutropenia/sepsis.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Carcinogenesis: growth signaling increases, tumor-suppressor function decreases, and DNA damage accumulates.
Invasion/metastasis: tumor crosses tissue boundaries and spreads through lymphatic or blood routes.
Primary care role: prevention, guideline-based screening, early recognition, diagnostic evaluation, coordination, symptom management, and safety-netting.
Never miss: new focal neurologic deficit with cancer/back pain, fever during significant immune suppression, airway/venous obstruction symptoms, severe metabolic symptoms, major bleeding, VTE symptoms, or rapidly declining function.
